newsitem.title: USA: Senior Republican calls on Gingrich to step down.
newsitem.headline: Senior Republican calls on Gingrich to step down.

text.p: Newt Gingrich's campaign to be re-elected speaker of the House of Representatives despite admitted ethics violations took a sharp blow Monday, the eve of the vote, when a senior Republican urged him to step aside.

In a statement issued as Gingrich returned to Washington to take charge of rallying the party troops for Tuesday's vote, Rep James Leach of Iowa, chairman of the House Banking Committee, said Gingrich was too tainted by ethics breaches to hold so prestigious and powerful a post as the speakership and the majority Republicans should elect someone else.
Leach's office said he would "vote for another Republican" -- the first such crack in the ranks of the House Republican leadership. There was no indication who his choice might be.

Nonetheless Gingrich was smiling broadly as he returned to the Capitol from his Georgia home base, and told a horde of reporters he remained "absolutely" confident of re-election in Tuesday's House vote. A handful of tourists applauded him.

Before Leach only one person in the 227-member House Republican delegation had stated he would not vote for Gingrich. That was Representative Michael Forbes of New York, a junior member about to start his second congressional term.

In a long statement, Leach said in part: "The occupant of this position must be free of any shadow concerning allegiance to the law or to the truth. Accordingly, for the country's sake I have concluded that the most responsible course of action for the speaker is to step down and for the members to choose another leader for the House."

Last December 21 Gingrich admitted that he had brought discredit on the House by not doing enough to prevent the use of tax-exempt donations in a partisan political activity -- in this case a college course he conducted titled "Renewing American Civilisation -- and by misleading ethics committee investigators looking into that matter.

A sore point among Democrats and some other Gingrich critics is that the speakership vote will take place one day before the ethics committee begins the process of considering punishments for him. That process is scheduled to run about two weeks before the full House renders its decision.
While many expected he would get off with a reprimand, the mildest available punishment, even that would make Gingrich the first sitting speaker ever punished by House vote.
Leach is widely respected among his colleagues as an intelligent, principled member of the House but one who often steers an independent course.
As banking chairman, he led a House investigation into the Whitewater business and ethics controversy involving President Bill Clinton and Hillary Rodham Clinton.

Leach drew a parallel to Clinton's troubles on Monday, saying, "It is self-evident that a critical way for the Republican Party to contrast itself with this administration is to set uncompromising ethical standards and insist on appropriate and timely accountability for its members."

Leach's decision to oppose Gingrich's re-election sharply increased the pressure on the Georgian and his allies to nail down party support at a closed meeting with his Republican colleagues later on Monday.
He is seeking to become the first Republican speaker to be re-elected in 68 years.

Republican leaders held conference calls among their colleagues to try to win over any waverers and sought in television appearances to portray the ethics controversy as a partisan assault by Democrats.

On the punishment issue, speculation has centred on the committee recommending to the full House that Gingrich suffer a reprimand, the third level of punishment below expulsion and censure. A censure could force him to step down as speaker.

The Capitol Hill newspaper Roll Call quoted an unnamed source on Monday as saying a four-member ethics subcommittee that investigated the Gingrich case is united in a decision to refer the tax-exempt funds matter to the criminal investigation division of the Internal Revenue Service.
